title: The hand is a metaphor
hook: God's "hand" and "eye" are figures of speech

segments.voice: Yesterday, silence is praise: Rabbi Hanina's question, and saying what God is not. When something moved you, did you let a breath say it instead of a word? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

"For with a strong hand hath the LORD brought thee out of Egypt." That line is in the Torah, and it's written inside the tefillin some Jews bind on the arm and head. A strong hand. For some readers, an image comes with it: an enormous arm reaching down out of the clouds. Maimonides spent real effort trying to take that picture down. And a scholar who read him closely pushed back, not on the picture, but on how harshly to judge the people who kept it. Today's word is where that argument starts.
screen: `A STRONG HAND.` → `AN ARM FROM THE CLOUDS?` → `A PICTURE TO TAKE DOWN.`

segments.voice: The hand is a metaphor. Turn it four ways. First, the list. In the opening laws of the Mishneh Torah, Maimonides gathers the Torah's bodily words for God: under God's feet, written with God's finger, the hand of the LORD, the eyes of the LORD, the ears of the LORD. All of these, he says, are spoken according to what human minds can grasp. God has no body. Second, what each organ is doing. In the Guide he explains the pattern. An eye stands for perceiving, an ear for hearing, a hand for acting. So when the Psalm says, "The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous," it means God's care reaches them. And the strong hand that brought Israel out of Egypt means God's power at work. The picture points at an action, not a limb. Third, the stakes. Maimonides doesn't treat this as a side issue. In his Laws of Repentance he lists someone who says God has a body or form among those who deny a core belief. Fourth, the pushback. Rabbi Abraham ben David, known as the Raavad, wrote short critical notes on the Mishneh Torah. On this line he wrote, in effect: why call such a person that? People greater and better than he followed this idea, because of what they read in the verses and in the midrash. The Raavad wasn't saying God has a body. He was defending the sincere reader who took the words plainly. Printed editions of the code carry his notes beside it. The code, and a reader who argued with it, side by side.
screen: `FEET, FINGER, HAND, EYES, EARS.` · `EACH PICTURE POINTS AT AN ACTION.` · `FOR MAIMONIDES, A CORE BELIEF.` · `THE RAAVAD DEFENDS THE PLAIN READER.` · then, large: `THE HAND IS A METAPHOR.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind one verse with a bodily picture of God in it. The strong hand. The eyes toward the righteous. God's ear, or God's arm. Hold the picture for a moment, just as it is. Then reread it the way Maimonides would. Ask: what action is this picture pointing at? Power? Attention? Listening? Say the verse again with that meaning in place of the limb. Notice whether it feels farther away, or closer. The bell holds the time.
The hand is a metaphor. Maimonides' teaching that God's hand, eyes and ears in scripture are figures for God's acting, caring and hearing, since God has no body. Today's word.
screen: `THE HAND IS A METAPHOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the hand is a metaphor. Today, catch one body word you use for something bigger, like lending a hand or keeping an eye out, and notice what action it really means. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Students of the Mishneh Torah read Maimonides' text together with the Raavad's printed glosses, weighing both. Some commentators on the Torah also explain bodily words for God as figures of speech.
